meta.title: Who really said "You can never cross the ocean until you have the courage to lose sight of the shore"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Columbus. It's a loose paraphrase of André Gide's novel Les Faux-monnayeurs (1925) — and Gide wrote the line about literature, not sailing.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You can never cross the ocean until you have the courage to lose sight of the shore'?
meta.ogDescription: Columbus never wrote it. The line paraphrases André Gide (1925) — from a scene where another character invokes Columbus a breath earlier.

answer.label: Not Columbus — a paraphrase of André Gide
answer.authorDates: 1869–1951 · French novelist · Nobel Prize in Literature, 1947
answer.sourceLine: Columbus never wrote or said this. The line is a loosened English paraphrase of a sentence from André Gide’s novel Les Faux-monnayeurs (1925), where the character Édouard says “One doesn’t discover new lands without consenting to lose sight of the shore for a very long time” — about literature, not seafaring. Columbus is named in the same exchange, but as an example raised by the other man in the conversation a breath earlier ↗, which may well be how the explorer’s name got stuck to it.

source.heading: The real source

docMeta.dd: 1925 · Éditions de la Nouvelle Revue Française, Paris
Part III, Chapitre XIV in the 1925 French (= Third Part, ch. XV in Bussy’s 1927 translation) — Édouard, interrupting Bernard
Dorothy Bussy, The Counterfeiters (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1927)

source.excerpt:
“I am afraid you don’t understand. When Columbus discovered America did he know towards what he was sailing? His goal was to go ahead, straight in front of him. Himself was his goal, impelling him to go ahead.…”

“I have often thought,” interrupted Edouard, “that in art, and particularly in literature, the only people who count are those who launch out on to unknown seas. One doesn’t discover new lands without consenting to lose sight of the shore for a very long time. But our writers are afraid of the open; they are mere coasters.”
trail: 1925 — the origin. Gide publishes Les Faux-monnayeurs. In Part III, Chapitre XIV, Édouard tells Bernard: “On ne découvre pas de terre nouvelle sans consentir à perdre de vue, d’abord et longtemps, tout rivage.” The scene is an argument about literary courage — and Bernard has just invoked Columbus. The 1925 text at French Wikisource ↗

1927 — into English. Dorothy Bussy’s translation for Knopf renders it “One doesn’t discover new lands without consenting to lose sight of the shore for a very long time.” Still no ocean to cross, still no courage. Bussy’s translation at Project Gutenberg ↗

The drift. The sentence loosens in circulation. Wikiquote records the sourced Gide line and notes it is “often misquoted” as “Man cannot discover new oceans unless he has the courage to lose sight of the shore” — and that it is “frequently misattributed to Christopher Columbus.” Wikiquote’s André Gide entry ↗

Today. The paraphrase circulates on quote sites, posters and LinkedIn under Columbus’s name. Wikiquote lists it under his Misattributed heading, with variants including “You can never cross the ocean unless you have the courage to lose sight of the shore,” and the verdict: “Actually by André Gide.” Wikiquote’s Columbus entry ↗
source.cutTag: Bussy tr., Third Part, ch. XV
source.excerptNote: Bernard speaks first; Édouard cuts him off. Dorothy Bussy’s 1927 translation. The famous sentence is Édouard’s — and it is about writers, not navigation. In the 1925 French: “On ne découvre pas de terre nouvelle sans consentir à perdre de vue, d’abord et longtemps, tout rivage.”

source.useLine: Free to use in the US, including in commercial and paid presentations. Bussy’s 1927 translation — the wording excerpted here — may still be in copyright outside the US, where terms run from the translator’s death in 1960. The popular paraphrase is too short and too unfixed in origin to carry a live claim, but it isn’t Gide’s wording, so don’t credit it to him.
source.rightsNote: Gide’s French original was published in 1925 and Dorothy Bussy’s English translation — the wording excerpted here — in 1927; both are comfortably pre-1931, and Project Gutenberg records the Bussy translation as “Public domain in the USA” ↗. Note that the popular one-line paraphrase is not Gide’s wording and has no identifiable author or source — it is simply a loose reworking of this public-domain text.

author.name: André Gide
author.heading: Who was André Gide?
author.metaLine: 1869–1951 · French novelist, critic and diarist · Nobel Prize in Literature, 1947
author.bio: André Gide was a French novelist, critic and diarist whose career ran from the Symbolist movement of the 1890s to sharp criticism of European colonialism between the wars; he was awarded the 1947 Nobel Prize in Literature and was called in his New York Times obituary “France’s greatest contemporary man of letters.” Les Faux-monnayeurs (1925) is his most ambitious novel — a novel-within-a-novel whose writer-character Édouard is generally read as Gide’s alter ego. The shore sentence is Édouard’s manifesto for risk-taking in art, which is exactly why it survives so well as free-floating advice once it is cut loose from the book that produced it.

cite.sourceCitation: André Gide, Les Faux-monnayeurs (Paris: Éditions de la Nouvelle Revue Française, 1925), pt. 3, chap. 14; translated by Dorothy Bussy as The Counterfeiters (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1927), Third Part, chap. 15 — the Bussy edition numbers the chapter one higher than the French.

misattribution.heading: Who it isn't
misattribution.intro: This one fails twice over: it names the wrong author, and it quotes words nobody actually wrote.

items.why: Columbus never wrote or said this, and no primary source connects him to it. Wikiquote files it under his Misattributed heading, records the variant “You can never cross the ocean unless you have the courage to lose sight of the shore,” and concludes flatly: “Actually by André Gide.” Wikiquote ↗

items.who: Nobody — it is an anonymous paraphrase
items.why: Gide wrote about discovering new lands by consenting to lose sight of the shore “for a very long time.” The popular sentence swaps in crossing an ocean and summoning courage — neither word appears in Gide. Wikiquote also flags a second common mangling, “Man cannot discover new oceans unless he has the courage to lose sight of the shore.” Wikiquote’s sourced Gide entry ↗

It is not about sailing at all. Édouard’s point is that “in art, and particularly in literature, the only people who count are those who launch out on to unknown seas… But our writers are afraid of the open; they are mere coasters.” The sea is a metaphor for literary risk. Bussy’s translation ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Gide’s, from Les Faux-monnayeurs (1925) — but the sentence people quote is a paraphrase of it, and the explorer in the passage is a rhetorical example raised by a character, not the author of the line. Read the passage in the 1925 text ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Gide’s line arrives in the middle of an argument about how to live. Bernard — just out of his exams, voluntarily homeless, casting about for a purpose — asks Édouard how a person is meant to choose a goal he cannot yet see, and reaches for the obvious example: “When Columbus discovered America did he know towards what he was sailing?” Édouard interrupts him. He is not interested in navigation. He is interested in writers.

That interruption is the quiet joke buried in the misattribution. The one name in the passage that is emphatically not the speaker’s is Columbus’s — it is a figure of speech raised by the other man in the room, and Édouard talks straight past it to make a point about literary nerve. Sand the sentence down into something printable over a photograph of a sunset, and the borrowed name is the part that survives.
detailsBody: Columbus’s surviving words come mainly from his letters and from the journal of the first voyage, which reaches us largely through a summary made by Bartolomé de Las Casas — Wikiquote flags exactly this provenance on its sourced entries. What is there is logbook prose: landfalls, green trees and streams of water, the people he met and coolly proposed to subjugate with fifty men. It is not aphorism, and nothing in it resembles this line. Wikiquote’s Columbus entry ↗

Columbus is a repeat magnet for this sort of thing. The same Wikiquote section flags “Following the light of the sun, we left the old world” as another line posted on blogs without citation — noting that the term ‘old world’ only originated around 1596, decades after Columbus’s death. Wikiquote’s Columbus entry ↗
